France: strike and protests against the cost of living, 575,000 people on the streets according to the Interior Ministry, 1.6 million according to the CGT

On Thursday 5 November, unions called for a strike and protests across France against the cost of living. The Interior Ministry counted 575,000 demonstrators (600,000 at 5 p.m.), the CGT nearly 1.6 million, including 350,000 in Paris; 448 arrests according to the ministry [1][7][8].

The call is backed by a broad inter-union alliance (CFDT, CGT, FO, UNSA, FSU and Solidaires). It demands a general rise in wages, pensions and the minimum wage, and a higher index point for civil servants' pay, according to AFP [3][4].

The Interior Ministry first counted about 600,000 demonstrators at 5 p.m. in 180 marches, a provisional figure later put at 575,000; the CGT claims nearly 1.6 million, including 350,000 in Paris. In Paris the ministry counts 65,000; in Marseille the police prefecture counts 14,000 against 150,000 according to the CGT [1][7][8]. At noon, the ministry's entourage mentioned 270,000 people and the CGT more than 250,000 at 1 p.m.: these first counts, taken at different times, were provisional [1][2].

Before the day, a security source expected between 500,000 and 700,000 demonstrators outside Paris and up to 80,000 in the capital [5]. For comparison: the ministry counted 550,000 people on 17 October and 410,000 on 24 October, when the CGT claimed nearly 800,000 [2].
Transport is affected: the four representative unions at SNCF are calling a strike, with possible disruption to TGV, Intercités and TER trains [3][4].

In education, the ministry reported nearly 16% of teachers on strike and 33% of higher-education institutions disrupted [1][2]. For the first time, all the unions in state-contracted private schools are also calling a strike [4].
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez announced that police and gendarmes would again be mobilised, about 70,000 in total [2].

What comes next is unclear: the yellow vests movement talks of renewing blockades on 6 and 7 November, but the unions, except Solidaires, are not for now talking of extending the strike beyond Thursday [4][6].

Key point: the anger no longer comes only from young people. For weeks, young people have demonstrated against the cost of living; on Thursday it is employees, with all the major confederations united, which is rare and gives the movement a weight that isolated days lacked [3][4].

The economic driver is simple: prices are rising faster than wages for part of the population. The demands (minimum wage, pensions, civil servants' index point) therefore target household budgets directly, and the State is involved twice: as employer of its civil servants and as the legislator of the minimum wage and pensions [3][4].

Turnout figures are a political issue in themselves. The ministry and the CGT almost always give very different totals, and the battle of numbers is used to say whether the movement is growing or fading. The earlier days (550,000 on 17 October, 410,000 on 24 October according to the ministry) serve as a benchmark: a total above 410,000 on Thursday evening would signal a rebound [2].

The ministry's end-of-day count (575,000) is higher than the two previous days (550,000 on 17 October, 410,000 on 24 October): by the official count, it is the strongest turnout in the series. The ministry's and the CGT's figures remain very far apart, as always [1][7][8].
If you take the train or have children at school, check right now for disruptions announced by your operator and your school: they could last until Friday if the movement is renewed.

United Kingdom: the Bank of England raises its rate to 4%, its first hike since 2023, because of energy

On Thursday 5 November, the Bank of England raised its policy rate by 0.25 points, from 3.75% to 4%, by 8 votes to 1. It is its first hike since 2023. Governor Andrew Bailey warns that the conflict in the Middle East could call for more [1][2][3].

The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) decided on Thursday 5 November to raise the policy rate to 4%, from 3.75% before, by 8 votes to 1 [1][2]. Only one member, Catherine Mann, wanted more: a 0.50-point rise, to 4.25% [1][2].

All nine members were therefore in favour of tightening; the disagreement is about its size. That is the meaning of City AM's "unanimous" headline, which refers to the direction of the decision, not the detail of the vote [1].
In September, the bank had held its rate at 3.75% by 6 votes to 3, with three members already calling for an immediate hike. The switch therefore happened within a single quarter [4][5].

The driver of the decision: energy. Disrupted supplies pushed up fuel prices and household energy bills. UK inflation was 3.5% in September, and the bank sees it rising to around 5% by mid-2027 [1][3].

Governor Andrew Bailey warned against the idea of an "inevitable long sequence of hikes", while adding that "unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved", this hike does not seem likely to be the last either [1].

Markets expected it: before the meeting, they gave more than a 96% chance of a hike; Bank of America forecast two 0.25-point hikes, in November and then February, to reach 4.25% [5][6]. Result: little immediate reaction in stock and bond markets, according to MoneyWeek [3].

Key point: a central bank that raises rates while the economy suffers an external shock chooses to fight inflation before growth. More expensive energy is not caused by the British, but if prices rise everywhere and wages and prices follow, inflation sets in. The bank therefore raises rates to break that spiral [1][3].

The mechanism: a higher policy rate makes credit more expensive (mortgages, business loans), which slows demand and price rises. It is the same reasoning as the ECB's, whose next meeting is on 17 December.

The detail of the vote matters as much as the hike: 8 to 1, with one vote for 0.50 points, leans "hawkish". Analysts had warned that the pound's reaction would depend on this split and on Bailey's tone. We found no move in the pound after the announcement, so we give none [3].

If you live, study or work in the United Kingdom, or have a variable-rate loan tied to the Bank of England's rate, your payment may go up. In France nothing changes directly, but it is one more signal that Europe's central banks are hardening their tone over energy.

Zillow plunges 16%: the property site forecasts fewer sales than expected, and its stock has already lost almost half this year

Zillow, the big American property listings site, published its third-quarter results on Wednesday 4 November: $724 million in sales (+7%), but below expectations, and a cautious outlook for the end of the year. The stock fell about 16% after the close [1][2][3].
According to Zillow's release, third-quarter sales rose 7% year on year to $724 million, against about $753 million expected by analysts (TipRanks) [1][2].
Adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.55, below the $0.58 expected. Under standard accounting (GAAP), Zillow reports a net loss of $158 million, or $0.70 per share [2].
For the fourth quarter, the company expects between $635 million and $665 million in sales, a range below what analysts hoped for [2].
The causes cited: high mortgage rates and a still-weak US housing market weighing on its residential business, and falling traffic on its site [2].
Adjusted earnings exclude a $165 million settlement tied to the shareholder class action over Zillow Offers, its former home-flipping business [1].
CNBC listed Zillow (more than 16%) among the biggest after-hours losers on Wednesday, alongside Expedia (more than 7%) [3]. Since January, Zillow's stock has already lost 48.6% [2].

Key point: on the stock market, a company is judged on what it promises to earn, not on what it has just earned. Zillow's sales are up 7%, but because analysts expected more and the outlook is lower than they hoped, the stock falls: the market revises future earnings down [2][3].

Zillow lives off housing: listings, advertising to estate agents, loans. When mortgage rates stay high, fewer households buy, so fewer visits and less revenue. It is a barometer of the US housing market's health, tied to Federal Reserve decisions [2].

Falling site traffic is a second signal: fewer visitors means fewer contacts to sell to agents. A worry similar to Reddit's this week, which is losing traffic to Google's artificial-intelligence answers.

Nothing to do directly: this story explains why a good sales figure is not enough to lift a stock. If you follow US property, it is one more sign that demand is still held back by the cost of credit. It is not advice to buy or sell.

How it works: why a disappointing outlook sends a stock plunging

A stock's price reflects what investors think the company will earn in the years ahead. Analysts publish expectations (revenue, earnings per share); when the company does less, it is a "miss". The outlook the company gives for the next quarter (guidance) often matters more than the past quarter: if it is below expectations, investors revise future earnings down, and the price falls straight away. After the close, trading is called "extended hours": the move can fade or grow the next day [2][3].

news.2026-11-05-egypte-fmi-programme-fin: Egypt: the IMF programme ends in December, and the Middle East war weighs on the Suez Canal

The IMF's lending programme for Egypt ends in December 2026, after five programmes since 2016 worth nearly $30 billion. On 2 November, Cairo signed a $1 billion loan with the World Bank, as the war weighs on its foreign-currency earnings [1][2][3].
According to the think tank TIMEP, the current IMF programme ends in December 2026. Since 2016, Egypt has received IMF financing under five programmes, for a total of nearly $30 billion [1].
On 2 November, Egypt signed a $1 billion deal with the World Bank, as the war worsens its economic difficulties, The National reports [2].

In a 21 September article, the IMF says Egypt's policy response helped it absorb the spillovers of the Middle East war, while noting that significant vulnerabilities remain. It also notes a gradual recovery in Suez Canal activity after disruptions [3].

Key point: the Suez Canal is one of Egypt's main sources of foreign currency, and the Middle East war reduces its revenue. Figures differ by source, between $4.4 and $4.7 billion recently, against nearly $10 billion before the Red Sea attacks [1][3]. Less foreign currency means more difficulty paying for imports and debt.

The end of the IMF programme marks a turning point: it served as an anchor for reforms and to reassure lenders. The question, debated on 16 November by TIMEP, is whether Egypt should request a new one [1].
If you follow energy or shipping prices, the Suez Canal is a link in the chain: fewer ships passing through means longer and costlier journeys for goods bound for Europe.

news.2026-11-05-chine-minerais-critiques: China: Beijing buys foreign mines to keep control of critical minerals

According to CNBC, China is expanding its stakes in mines abroad to tighten its grip on critical minerals. It produces about 92% of the world's refined rare earths, according to the International Energy Agency, but host countries are starting to restrict exports of raw ore [1].
CNBC reports on 4 November that Beijing is widening its stakes in mines outside China [1].
China produces about 92% of the world's refined rare earths, according to the International Energy Agency cited by CNBC [1].
Countries hosting these mines are reacting: they restrict exports of unprocessed ore and require foreign partners to refine locally [1].

In September, China exported 4,269.8 tonnes of rare earths, 6.7% more than a year earlier; over the first nine months, exports are still down 9.6%, at 43,711 tonnes, according to customs data cited by Reuters [2].

Key point: China's advantage lies not only in mines but above all in refining, the step that makes minerals usable. By buying mines and keeping the refining, Beijing controls the chain end to end. Producer countries in turn want to keep that step at home [1].

The one-year suspension of China's October 2025 export controls runs until 10 November 2026; no Chinese extension has been published to date, even though Washington mentions a truce until 10 January 2027 [2][3]. China's Commerce Ministry said in October it would keep approving licences for Europe, whatever happens to the deal with the United States [3].
Rare earths go into electric-car motors, wind turbines and phones: a squeeze on their supply can, in time, make these products more expensive.

Argentina: country risk tops 900 points as bonds and stocks slide after the US elections

On Thursday 5 November, Argentina's country risk, measured by JP Morgan, crossed the 900-point mark, between 915 and 927 depending on the outlet, its highest since October 2025. Dollar bonds lost up to 3.7%, the Merval 3% to 4.2% and Mercado Libre 14% [1][2][3][4].

Country risk, which measures the gap between what Argentina pays to borrow in dollars and what the United States pays, rose from 852 points at Wednesday's close to 915-927 on Thursday, according to the outlets consulted; iProfesional reports an intraday peak of 982 before a pullback to 927 [1][3][5].
It is the highest level since 24 October 2025, according to Cadena 3. On 3 November it stood at 829 points, against a low of 403 on 7 July [4][6].
Sovereign dollar bonds fell by as much as 3.5-3.7%; the 2038 and 2035 Globales were among the hardest hit, according to Rosario Finanzas [3][5].

The Merval lost between 3% (85,628 points) and 4.2% (84,564 points) depending on the time and outlet; Mercado Libre, the big e-commerce company listed on Wall Street, plunged 14% after publishing its quarterly results [2][4].

An analyst at Oficina de Inversiones, quoted by La Nación, mainly blames a global factor: Wall Street fell again after Wednesday's rebound, which had followed the Democratic win in the US midterm elections [2].

Economy Minister Luis Caputo said the US election result would not substantially change the bilateral relationship; the market is watching the deadlines: about $1.3 billion owed to the IMF between November and December, and $4.4 billion to bondholders in January, according to the Argentine press [3][5].

Key point: country risk is the thermometer of lenders' confidence. When it rises, Argentina must offer a higher yield to borrow in dollars, and beyond about 900 points investors start to wonder whether the country can repay without outside help [1][3].

The shock comes from two sides. Abroad, Wall Street's decline reduces appetite for emerging countries; at home, analysts fear that the Democratic win in Congress will limit Donald Trump's room to help Javier Milei, even though Washington has opened a $20 billion currency swap line with Buenos Aires and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said he is ready to buy Argentine bonds if needed [6][7].

The central bank's gross reserves stood at $50.3 billion on 3 November and it had not bought any dollars since the start of the month: the country has little room to meet dollar payments if markets close to it [8].
The drop in Mercado Libre, Latin America's top listed company in its category in New York, shows that the sell-off also hits private companies, not just the state [4].

If you have family or savings in Argentina, remember that the peso and the country's debt react as much to Wall Street and Washington as to Buenos Aires. For a European reader the direct effect is small, but it is a test: an emerging country heavily indebted in dollars is the first to suffer when the US stock market falls.

CVS Health plans to split in two, pharmacies on one side, Aetna insurance on the other, and its shares fall 13%

On Wednesday 4 November, CVS Health announced it would split into two listed companies: its roughly 9,000 pharmacies on one side, insurer Aetna and drug-benefit management on the other. The shares fell about 12.6% to $79.94, with investors seeing a defensive move [1][2][3].

The company keeping the CVS Health name will group Aetna, the pharmacy benefit manager Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health and Signify Health; David Joyner, chairman and chief executive, keeps his roles there [1][2].
The second, CVS Pharmacy, will take the roughly 9,000 stores, the mail-order pharmacy, MinuteClinic and Health100, with Prem Shah, currently group president, as chief executive [2].
The separation is expected in the first half of 2028, subject to final board approval; shareholders would receive shares in both companies tax-free, according to the company [2].

According to Reuters, the stock plunged 12.6% to $79.94; other outlets say 12% to 13%. UBS analyst Kevin Caliendo says the announcement was a surprise and is seen as a defensive move against regulation rather than an offensive one [1][3].
David Joyner presents the plan as a decision taken “from a position of strength”, citing the recovery of Aetna's Medicare business and good pharmacy results, despite a solid third quarter [2][3].

A bipartisan bill, the Patients Before Monopolies Act, would bar a company that owns an insurer or a benefit manager from also owning a pharmacy; analysts also cite debt and the dividend as open questions [2][4].

Key point: on the stock market a split is often welcomed when it unlocks value, but here the market punished the announcement because it reads it as a response to political pressure, not a strategic choice [1][3].

CVS is a rare case: the company sells drugs at the counter, insures millions of patients and negotiates drug prices for other insurers. That vertical integration is exactly what the bill targets. By separating the two businesses, CVS lowers the risk of an abrupt ban, but loses the synergies that justified the whole [2][3].
The timeline, 2028, is long: until then the company must split its debt between the two firms and decide the fate of the dividend, two points analysts see as unresolved [4].

Nothing to do directly: this story explains why a split announcement can push a stock down. If you follow US healthcare, it is a sign that the “insurer + pharmacy + drug-benefit manager” model is under political pressure. This is not advice to buy or sell.

How it works: a spin-off, and why the stock can rise or fall

In a spin-off, a company separates a business into a distinct company and distributes its shares to existing shareholders: each then owns two stocks instead of one. The theory: each company, simpler to understand, can be better valued, and its management focuses on one business. But the market also looks at the why. If the split looks forced (pressure from regulators or activist shareholders), it sees a defensive move and the price falls. It also depends on debt: one of the two companies may inherit a heavier load. The trade-off is that a company that splits loses the savings its size gave it [1][3][5][6].
When big groups split up
2 April 2024
General Electric splits: on the first trading day, the new GE Vernova loses $2 to $140 after an early rally, while GE Aerospace falls more than 18% to $136 [5].
The old company's price falls mechanically by the weight of what leaves: value must be judged across the two stocks together.
April 2024

After its separation, GE Vernova gains more than 20% within days while GE Aerospace falls about 5%, whereas Solventum, spun off from 3M, drops because of its debts and the stake kept by its parent [6].
A split succeeds or not depending on the debt inherited and the number of shares the parent can still sell.

NextDC soars 51%: Goodman and Digital Realty quietly buy nearly 10% of the Australian data-centre giant

On Thursday 5 November, shares in Australian data-centre group NextDC closed up 50.8% after Goodman Group and US-based Digital Realty acquired up to 9.9% of its capital at A$9.50 a share, 45% above the previous close [1][2][3].

The purchase goes through a joint vehicle, Ackland Investments No.1, owned equally by Goodman and Digital Realty, which ran an aftermarket bookbuild (a placement after the close) on Wednesday to buy up to 9.9% of NextDC at A$9.50 a share [1][3].
That price is 45% above Wednesday's close of A$6.53; according to Reuters, citing an investor document, the deal is worth about A$715 million, or US$501 million [1][3].
NextDC's board called the move “opportunistic” and said it does not know the outcome; the buyers said they do not currently intend to make a control bid, while reserving the right to do so [3].
According to CNBC, the stock closed up 50.84% on Thursday; during the session, other outlets reported 43% (A$9.34) then 45.8% (A$9.52) [1][3].

NextDC had lost more than 40% since January, mostly in late October when it paused all future developments and cut its revenue forecasts; even after the rise, the stock is still about 37% below its level a year ago [3].
The deal comes as US data-centre stocks fell the day before, on fears of tighter oversight after the Democratic win in the midterm elections [3].

Key point: when an investor buys a big stake in a listed company without taking it over, the price rises because other shareholders wonder whether it will go further. Here the price paid (A$9.50) has become a reference floor [1][3].

Data centres, where artificial-intelligence services are stored and run, have become a highly sought-after asset: computing infrastructure is scarce and building it is expensive. Goodman, a logistics property group, and Digital Realty, one of the world's big players, are betting that a weakened NextDC is worth more than its previous price [3].

Stakes below the 10% threshold are a classic step before an offer: they let a buyer enter the capital without having to launch a full public offer, while hampering a possible rival bid. It remains to be seen whether Goodman and Digital Realty will go further [3].
Nothing to do directly: this story shows how the appetite to own data centres, at the heart of AI, can push even a struggling stock up by half in one session. This is not advice to buy or sell.

How it works: why buying a 9.9% stake makes a stock jump

Buying nearly 10% of a company is a waiting position: the buyer can stay a shareholder or later move towards a takeover offer. The market does two calculations: a buyer paying a 45% premium sets a reference price, and a large buyer may come back. Other shareholders then stop selling below that price, and the stock often rises to the price paid. The opposite risk: if the buyer backs off, the premium can deflate. The target's board can also resist by calling the move opportunistic, as here [1][3].

news.2026-11-05-tunisie-algerie-zone-lib: Tunisia and Algeria open talks on a free-trade zone at their border

On Thursday 5 November, Tunisian Trade Minister Samir Abid announced that Tunis and Algiers had begun talks to create a free-trade zone at their shared border. Four draft agreements are on the table, according to La Presse de Tunisie [1].

According to La Presse de Tunisie, the talks cover four draft agreements: an economic partnership agreement, an agreement on mutual recognition of conformity certificates, an agreement on goods transit and a sector agreement on automotive components [1].
The idea is not new: in June 2026, Chadhli Maï, an official at Tunisia's trade ministry, said a study of a free commercial and logistics zone along the border had just been completed [2].

Maghreb Émergent also reports that the two governments talk of border free-trade zones “soon”; the existing preferential agreement between the two countries is being evaluated for an upgrade to a free-trade agreement [3].
Key point: a border free-trade zone aims to replace informal trade, often smuggling, with declared trade, with lower tariffs and checks recognised on both sides [1][3].

For Tunisia, which borders Algeria to the west and Libya to the east, it is a way to widen outlets while its border regions suffer from unemployment; for Algeria, it is an opening to its neighbours, at a time when its trade with Morocco keeps falling [1][3].
If you follow the Maghreb, it is a sign of economic rapprochement between Tunis and Algiers. Nothing is signed: these are talks, and no conclusion date is announced in the sources consulted.

news.2026-11-05-mexique-douane-controles: Mexico: customs tightens checks on Asian imports under pressure from Washington

On Wednesday 4 November, Mexico's national customs agency (ANAM) announced tighter checks on imports from Asia, targeting false values and false origins. Washington wants stricter rules of origin in the review of the North American trade agreement [1].
ANAM targets goods whose value or origin is falsified; according to the Rio Times, it is unclear whether Washington will consider these checks sufficient in the review of the USMCA [1].

In that review, Mexico and Canada ask for a 16-year extension, while the United States proposes ten years with annual reviews; President Claudia Sheinbaum wants lower US tariffs on cars, steel and aluminium and no new tariffs during the talks [2][3].

More than 80% of Mexican exports to the United States, those that comply with the agreement's rules, enter tariff-free, according to Mexican officials: the stake is therefore keeping that regime [3].
If you buy products made in Mexico or follow the trade war, remember that the fate of the agreement turns on a technical detail: where each part really comes from.

Paraguay: President Santiago Peña resigns after the collapse of Ueno Bank, the guaraní loses 8%

On Thursday 5 November, Paraguayan President Santiago Peña resigned hours after the central bank intervened in Ueno Bank, the country's sixth-largest bank, which counted more than 60% of adults among its customers. The guaraní lost about 8% and country risk jumped [1][2][3].
The crisis began on 29 October 2026: Ueno Bank told the central bank of Paraguay (BCP) that it could not rebuild about $70 million of its required reserve, according to Infobae [3].

According to CBC, Santiago Peña resigned hours after the central bank took control of Ueno Bank, which had more than 60% of the country's adults as customers; La Nación (Costa Rica) speaks of three million Paraguayans cut off from their savings [2][4].
Bloomberg Línea describes Ueno as the country's sixth-largest bank and says the resignation came while the Chamber of Deputies was debating a request to impeach the president [1][6].
The accusations concern conflicts of interest: according to La Nación, Santiago Peña was a shareholder of Ueno Holding until 2025, when he left the company [4].
Eight bank executives have been arrested and the central bank's president, Carlos Carvallo, has also resigned [4].

Infobae reports a guaraní down about 8% and a sharp rise in Paraguay's country risk; the central bank and the banking association (Asoban) say the collapse does not affect the whole financial system [3][5].

According to Bloomberg Línea, Vice President Pedro Alliana would have taken over the presidency had Peña been removed; La Nación notes that the opposition also wanted an impeachment trial against him [1][4].

Key point: when a big bank fails, savers pay first. Ueno counted more than 60% of adults among its customers: the central bank's intervention therefore hit a very large share of the population, which explains how fast the political crisis moved [2][4].

The mechanism is classic. A bank must keep part of its deposits in reserve at the central bank (the required reserve). When it can no longer rebuild it, as Ueno could not on 29 October for about $70 million, the central bank steps in to avoid a panic: if everyone wants to withdraw their money at once, no bank can repay everybody [3].

A political question is added to the banking one: suspicion of a conflict of interest between the head of state and the bank turned a failure into a crisis of the regime. The central bank chief's departure and the arrest of eight executives show the affair touches both power and bank supervision [1][4].

Key point: placing assets under “temporary management” is a takeover without a change of official owner. The company keeps its shares, but the Russian state chooses who runs the factory and collects the profits, which often prepares a forced sale at a low price [1][3].

Russia uses its emergency laws to make “unfriendly” countries pay the price of sanctions, taking assets their companies cannot carry away [1][4].

Foreign investors still present in Russia get a warning: after distributors and consumer brands, an industrial manufacturer is targeted. These are concrete assets, factories and brands, that no foreign court ruling can protect on the spot [1][3].

If you work for a company that still has activities in Russia, or if you follow sanctions, remember that leaving the country can be costly: staying exposes a company to takeover, leaving often means selling at a very low price.

How it works: why an election result moves the stock market

A stock's price reflects what investors expect from future earnings, adjusted for risk. Some sectors also depend on specific decisions (energy, health, defense) and react according to what the new balance of power suggests. How it works: why gold reacts to the dollar and to interest rates

Gold is sold in dollars on global markets. If the dollar falls, a European or Asian buyer pays less in their own currency, and demand can increase. In addition, gold pays neither interest nor dividends: when rates rise, bonds and interest-bearing accounts pay more, and gold becomes less attractive; when rates fall or the dollar weakens, the opposite happens. Finally, gold is a safe haven, but not always: in the event of a sharp fall in stock markets, some investors sell it to raise cash elsewhere, which explains last week's abrupt drops [1][3][7].

news.2026-11-05-bresil-copom-selic-pause: Brazil: central bank pauses rate cuts at 13.75% after Lula's reelection

On Wednesday, November 4, the monetary policy committee (Copom) unanimously left the Selic rate at 13.75%, ending five cuts in a row. Reuters links the pause to the prospect of higher inflation after the reelection of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva [1][2].
The Copom, chaired by Gabriel Galípolo, voted unanimously to keep the Selic rate at 13.75%, after five consecutive cuts [1][3].
The decision was expected: 33 of the 48 economists polled by Reuters and 26 of 31 in a Bloomberg survey forecast a pause [1][2].
Before the meeting, inflation stood at 4.58% and the real was weaker; the rate remains about 9 points above inflation [3].
Officials raised their inflation forecast for 2027 to 4.7%, from 3.9% [2], and repeated that monetary policy must remain "substantially restrictive" [1].

Key takeaway: a central bank cuts rates when it considers prices under control. Here, it is stopping because the 2027 inflation forecast is rising, and because Lula's reelection, according to Reuters, raises fears of more public spending [1][2].
The Copom gave no signal about what comes next; its next meeting, on December 8 and 9, is the last of the year [3].

In Brazil, a high policy rate makes loans and purchases on credit more expensive; for a foreign investor, it makes investments in reais more rewarding but the currency more sensitive to political news.

According to the Korea Times, October exports reached $115.3 billion, a monthly record, up 93.7% over one year [1].

news.2026-11-05-chine-services-pmi-octob: China: services activity slows in October, to its lowest in three months
The RatingDog index of Chinese services activity fell to 50.8 in October, from 51.6 in September, below the 51.5 expected. It is its lowest since July, and business confidence declined [1][2].
The RatingDog services index (formerly Caixin) went from 51.6 in September to 50.8 in October; above 50, activity is growing, but more slowly [1][2][3].
Export orders continued to grow for the sixth month, but more slowly than in September [1].
Business costs rose at the fastest pace in five months, while firms cut their selling prices for the second month in a row, which weighs on their margins [1][3].
Business confidence fell to a three-month low [1][2].

Key takeaway: services, which cover retail, transport, finance and catering, are the main outlet for Chinese consumers. Their slowdown, with falling prices, shows domestic demand is still fragile [1][2].
This release adds to other signals: manufacturing activity fell back below 50 according to another tracker of October PMIs, which feeds the debate on supporting demand [4].
If your business sells in China (luxury, food products, tourism, machinery), soft domestic demand weighs on orders; conversely, falling Chinese prices may later show up in imported goods.
